h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר ט׳ Parshas Zachor — Maamar Tes

p: בַּפְּסִיקְתָּא (לְפָרָשַׁת זָכוֹר פָּרָשָׁה יב סִימָן יב)
In the Pesikta (for Parshas Zachor, Parsha 12, siman 12):
To what may the matter be compared?
To a king who had an orchard
and he had a certain dog, etc.
בָּא בְּנוֹ שֶׁל אוֹהֲבוֹ שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ
The son of the king's beloved friend came
to steal from within the orchard;
the dog rose up and bit him.
Whenever the king wished to remind
the son of his beloved friend
that he had wanted to steal,
And when HaKadosh Baruch Hu wished
to remind Yisrael of the sin
is to remember the sin and the cause
why did He not wish to mention
but only that they should remember the sin
And if it is in order not to mention their disgrace,
אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ בַּמִּדְבָּר וְגוֹמֵר [דְּבָרִים ט, ז]
Hashem your God in the wilderness," etc. (Devarim 9:7),
and He enumerated explicitly the Golden Calf
So why is it different here,
that He was sparing and did not wish
the matter of the command to remember
more than the sins of the other generations.
that there the mitzvah is to remember
the episode of the Calf, which befell them
where a maidservant saw at the Sea
the voice of the living God
and it is written (ibid. 5:4), "Face to face
for they saw what Yechezkel did not see
and nevertheless it was in the power
of the yetzer hara to enter their hearts
to so grave a transgression as this.
a person will be spurred to guard himself
from the enticements of the yetzer hara,
and he will not trust in his deeds
until the day of his death;
and this one must remember always.
This is like that incident with the chassid
until the day of your old age,
so that he would admit and teach,
פֶּרֶק ה דְּשַׁבָּת הֲלָכָה ג ח, א)
even though he certainly knew of himself
that his heart was slain within him
And so too David HaMelech, alav hashalom,
שֶׁאָמַר וְלִבִּי חָלַל בְּקִרְבִּי [תְּהִלִּים קט, כב]
who said, "And my heart is slain within me" (Tehillim 109:22),
וְאָמַר בְּחָנֵנִי ה׳ וְגוֹמֵר [שָׁם כו, ב]
and cried out, "Would that my mouth had not uttered it"
And regarding this it is said (Bamidbar 13:29),
"Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev,"
שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג קס, א)
about which they said in the holy Zohar (vol. 3, 160a)
that it alludes to the yetzer hara;
even in the soul of a person
to remember the episode of the Calf,
so that a person should not divert his mind
from guarding himself against the enticements of the yetzer hara
even when he is at the highest level,
This is not so regarding the sin
that caused the coming of Amalek,
about which they said in the holy Zohar
that they did not know this thing? etc.
they wished to know the difference
rather it lay in matters of secrets,
at something higher than their grasp,
"Into what is too wondrous for you do not inquire, etc.;
you have no business with hidden things."
And this is referred to by the name
and one who errs in this
is called "one who cut down the saplings"
And regarding this it is said
בְּכָל בֵּיתִי נֶאֱמָן הוּא [בַּמִּדְבָּר יב, ז]
in all My house he is trusted" (Bamidbar 12:7).
But what relevance has trustworthiness Above,
when there is no possibility of stealing
Rather, one who gazes at something
that does not belong to him
stealing from the house of the King,
not to take more than one's portion.
And this is what we say (Shabbos morning prayer),
"Moshe rejoiced in the gift of his portion,"
which he chose for Yisrael in Egypt,
and so the early authorities explained.
According to this we must understand
מַה שֶּׁאוֹמְרִים כִּי עֶבֶד נֶאֱמָן וְכוּלֵּי
what we say, "For a trusted servant," etc.,
which implies that it gives a reason.
But the intent is as above,
מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר לֹא כֵן עַבְדִּי וְגוֹמֵר
what is said, "Not so My servant," etc.,
"in all My house he is trusted;
and nevertheless he did not gaze
at what did not belong to his portion,
for this is the meaning of "he is trusted,"
And Shabbos is the time of the revelation of Atika,
and the morning is the time
and then is the time of the revelation of secrets,
in the song (the zemer Asader LiSeudasa):
"May He send us His splendor, etc.;
may He show us His hidden things,
may He reveal to us the reasons," etc.;
וְזֶהוּ כֹּחַ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And this is the power of Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom,
only at what one has been permitted,
what is fitting for the portion of the soul's root.
"Moshe rejoiced in the gift of his portion,"
and it is the time of the revelation of secrets,
and he is a trusted servant,
And this is what they said (Chagigah 14b)
regarding the four who entered the Pardes:
Ben Zoma gazed and was harmed,
the ministering angels sought to push away;
was not within what is permitted
and it is in hidden matters;
and HaKadosh Baruch Hu said to them,
that is, that this was within what he was permitted,
like the matter of "in all My house he is trusted,"
that he would not take more
than the portion of his root.
And this is precisely indicated in the parable,
שֶׁבָּא בְּנוֹ שֶׁל אוֹהֲבוֹ שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ
that the son of the king's beloved friend came
to steal from within the orchard;
that is, that they gazed at this,
which did not belong to them,
from within the Pardes, as mentioned above;
and through this the dog bit them,
Therefore it is not fitting to command
שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה חֵטְא פָּשׁוּט כָּל כָּךְ
for it was not so simple a sin,
as in the question of the holy Zohar,
to remember the deed of Amalek, which it caused.
And through this they will not break through
more than is fitting for them,
And it can be said that this is why the parable mentions
בְּנוֹ שֶׁל אוֹהֲבוֹ שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ דַּיְיקָא
specifically "the son of the king's beloved friend,"
the son of the king's beloved friend."
That is, the reason Yisrael craved
the children of Avraham Avinu, alav hashalom,
for the beginning of the revelation of secrets
was to Avraham Avinu, alav hashalom,
At first, "the secret of Hashem is for those who fear Him";
"And with the upright is His secret";
That is, one who fears Hashem
at what does not belong to him,
and Hashem Yisbarach reveals His secret to him;
וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
and so it is found regarding Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom
בִּשְׂכַר כִּי יָרֵא מֵהַבִּיט [שְׁמוֹת ג, ו]
in reward for "for he was afraid to look" (Shemos 3:6),
"and the image of Hashem does he behold" (Bamidbar 12:8).
who has no yetzer hara in him,
for his heart has already been made straight,
and he has only one heart
such a one certainly will not crave
to contemplate what he was not permitted,
and with him is the secret of Hashem,
that He reveals to him all the secrets.
And to a prophet Hashem Yisbarach reveals secrets
and not what is too wondrous for him,
"If there be a prophet among you, I Hashem
make Myself known to him in a vision," etc.;
that he is fit to grasp,
in the aspect of vision or dream.
in all My house he is trusted" (ibid. 7),
at what does not belong to him.
And this is because it is written of him beforehand,
וְהָאִישׁ מֹשֶׁה עָנָיו מְאֹד וְגוֹמֵר [שָׁם, ג]
"And the man Moshe was very humble," etc. (ibid. 3),
and every matter was great in his eyes
relative to himself, in accordance with his humility;
and therefore Hashem Yisbarach revealed to him
"Mouth to mouth do I speak," etc.,
"and the image of Hashem does he behold."
And to Avraham Avinu, alav hashalom,
upright among the upright, and a prophet,
for Hashem Yisbarach revealed secrets to him,
And likewise at the morning meal of Shabbos,
and the meal corresponds to the holiness
as the Arizal, zichrono livrachah, wrote
[פְּרִי עֵץ חַיִּים שַׁעַר הַשַּׁבָּת פֶּרֶק יז]
and all Yisrael merit to be crowned
with the holiness of Avraham Avinu, alav hashalom,
it is the time of the revelation of secrets,
And Yisrael merited at the Splitting of the Sea
as they said, "A maidservant saw," etc.,
because they are "the seed of Avraham My beloved."
And afterwards the light was concealed from them,
as they said in the holy Zohar
for they were seeking to gaze upon it,
even though it was before the giving of the Torah;
"and we have learned that Kudsha Brich Hu
that is, they sought the revelation
which they had had and which was hidden from them.
מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהֵם בְּנוֹ שֶׁל אוֹהֲבוֹ שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ
because they are the son of the king's beloved friend,
the children of Avraham Avinu, alav hashalom,
and since it was hidden from them,
that they yearned to gaze into
"Is Hashem in our midst or not (Ayin)"
than the portion given them to contemplate;
and this is what they said,
שֶׁבָּא בְּנוֹ שֶׁל אוֹהֲבוֹ שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ דַּיְיקָא
that specifically the son of the king's beloved friend came
to steal specifically from within the orchard,
And HaKadosh Baruch Hu did not wish
to mention the sin and to command
for this is not an explicit sin,
and who would know that this is a sin?
that the dog came and bit them,
and from this you will know the sin,
and you will take care not to contemplate
anything but what you have been permitted.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 82a, Yitro 19:17–18 — “Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Judah said: Israel saw here what Ezekiel son of Buzi did not see, and all cleaved to precious supernal wisdom. Israel saw five degrees of voices at Mount Sinai, and through these five degrees Torah was given. ... Rabbi Elazar said: Concerning Israel it is written, ‘Face to face the Lord spoke’; concerning Ezekiel it is written ‘like the appearance’ and ‘a likeness,’ like one looking through many walls. What Israel saw no other prophet saw; all the more so what Moses saw, no other prophet saw.” The passage distinguishes the directness of Sinai from Ezekiel’s mediated vision. This sharpens Rav Tzadok’s warning that even great revelation does not justify self-confidence.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a:2–3 — “Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: A person should never bring himself to a test, for David king of Israel brought himself to a test and stumbled. He said before Him: Master of the world, why do they say, ‘God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob,’ but not ‘God of David’? He said: They were tested by Me, and you were not tested by Me. He said before Him: Master of the world, examine me and test me, as it is said, ‘Examine me, Lord, and test me.’ He said: I will test you, and I will tell you something I did not tell them: I will test you in a matter of sexual transgression.” The Talmud makes David’s request an explicit warning against deliberately seeking a test. The manuscript’s further allusion to “I resolved that my mouth not transgress” belongs to its account of his regret.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 13a:2 — “Until here you have permission to speak; from here onward you have no permission to speak. For it is written in the book of Ben Sira: Do not investigate what is beyond you, and do not search out what is concealed from you. Contemplate what you have been permitted; you have no business with the hidden things.” The limitation concerns what one has been authorized and equipped to contemplate. Rav Tzadok describes overreaching that portion through the orchard’s image of theft.

paragraphs.text: Numbers 12:6-8 — “If there is a prophet among you, I, the Lord, make Myself known to him in a vision; in a dream I speak with him. Not so My servant Moses: in all My house he is faithful. Mouth to mouth I speak with him, in a clear appearance and not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the Lord.” The contrast between ordinary prophetic disclosure and Moses’ faithful standing in the divine house supplies Rav Tzadok’s language of an allotted share.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 1:28 — “‘He saw their burdens’: He saw that they had no rest. He went and said to Pharaoh: A person who owns a slave—if the slave does not rest one day in the week, he dies. These are your slaves; if you do not allow them one day in the week, they will die. He said to him: Go and do for them as you say. Moses went and established Shabbat for them to rest.” The Midrash gives the account of Moses choosing a day of rest while Israel were in Egypt.

paragraphs.text: Tur, Orach Chayim 281:1 — “The explanation of ‘Moses shall rejoice’: When our ancestors were in Egypt and Moses saw the heavy servitude imposed on them, he asked Pharaoh to give them one day in the week on which to rest. Pharaoh granted it to him, and he chose the seventh day. When they were commanded concerning Shabbat, Moses rejoiced that he had chosen it. This is ‘Moses shall rejoice in the gift of his portion.’” This identifies one of the earlier written explanations to which Rav Tzadok refers. The Tur also records a second explanation based on Shabbat as God’s good gift.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Beshalach 11 — “‘In all My house he is faithful’… one who restrains his mouth from speaking and his heart from musing; and this is ‘faithful,’ that he does not touch what is above his portion.” Rav Tzadok there grounds Moshe’s faithfulness in the “belimah” of Sefer Yetzirah: “if your heart runs, return to the place.” Through that silence and self-nullification (“what are we”), all the secrets were revealed to him.

paragraphs.text: Isaac Luria, Asader li-Seudata, stanzas 3–4,8 — “May He send us His beauty, and may we behold His glory; may He show us His secrets, which are spoken in a whisper. May He reveal to us the meanings within the twelve loaves, which are a letter in His name, doubled and subtle. ... To crown the table with a precious mystery, deep and hidden, and not a noisy utterance.” The song’s own language makes disclosure of secrets part of the morning Shabbat meal. The original Aramaic was checked in a digital transcription of the poem; no printed siddur edition is claimed.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 14b:8–9; 15b:16 — “The Sages taught: Four entered the orchard: Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Aher, and Rabbi Akiva. ... Ben Azzai looked and died. ... Ben Zoma looked and was harmed. ... Aher cut the plantings. Rabbi Akiva emerged in peace.” Chagigah 15b adds: “Rabbi Akiva ascended in peace and descended in peace. ... Even Rabbi Akiva—the ministering angels sought to thrust him away. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Leave this elder, for he is fit to make use of My glory.” The distinction turns on fitness for the encounter.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 49:2 — “At first, ‘the secret of the Lord’ was ‘for those who fear Him’; afterward, for the upright: ‘His secret is with the upright’; afterward, for the prophets: ‘He does nothing unless He has revealed His secret to His servants the prophets.’ The Holy One said: This Abraham fears God, as it is said, ‘Now I know that you fear God.’ This Abraham is upright among the upright. ... This Abraham is a prophet, as it is said, ‘Return the man’s wife, for he is a prophet.’ Shall I not reveal it to him?” The Midrash combines fear, uprightness, and prophecy in Abraham. Rav Tzadok develops the restraint appropriate to each as the condition for receiving a secret.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Moshe ben Maimon, Moreh Nevuchim I:5 — “A person should not rush into this great and sublime matter at his first encounter, before training himself in the sciences and knowledge, thoroughly refining his character, and subduing his appetites and imagined longings. After attaining true premises and learning the rules of inference and protection against errors of thought, he may begin the inquiry. He should not decide by his first impression or initially let his thoughts range toward apprehending the Deity; he should hold back in reverence until he advances gradually. This is the meaning of ‘Moshe hid his face, for he feared to gaze toward God.’ … That restraint was praised, and afterward he merited, ‘He beholds the likeness of Hashem.’”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Rambam connects restraint in divine inquiry to prior moral and intellectual preparation, and uses the same sequence from Moshe’s hidden face to his later vision. This explains why Rav Tzadok links fear of God and an upright heart with receiving secrets without taking what has not yet been allotted. Rambam describes readiness through training; Rav Tzadok speaks here of each soul’s allotted portion.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 3:1 — “Rabbi Joshua of Sikhnin said in the name of Rabbi Levi: Nevertheless, He showed him. In reward for ‘Moses hid his face,’ ‘The Lord spoke to Moses face to face.’ In reward for ‘for he feared,’ ‘They feared to approach him.’ In reward for ‘from looking,’ ‘He beholds the form of the Lord.’ ... Rabbi Hoshaya the elder said: He did well to hide his face. The Holy One said to him: I came to show you My face, and you honored Me and hid your face. By your life, you will be with Me on the mountain forty days and forty nights, without eating or drinking, and you will delight in the radiance of the Divine Presence.” The Midrash preserves a debate over Moses’ initial concealment and then articulates the positive relation between restraint and later disclosure.

paragraphs.text: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Shabbat 17:3 — “Before the Shabbos evening meal one says: This is the meal of the field of holy apples; Zeir Anpin and the Holy Ancient One come to dine with her. This meal belongs to Yitzchak, who is its master and directs it; one who delights in it is saved from the birth pangs of Mashiach. At the morning meal ... he says: This is the meal of the Holy Ancient One; Zeir Anpin and the field of holy apples come to dine with Him. It corresponds to Avraham, the pious elder, and through his merit one is saved from the judgment of Gehinnom.” The cited Lurianic text explicitly associates the morning meal with Abraham and the Holy Ancient One.

— “Before the Shabbos evening meal one says: This is the meal of the field of holy apples; Zeir Anpin and the Holy Ancient One come to dine with her. This meal belongs to Yitzchak, who is its master and directs it; one who delights in it is saved from the birth pangs of Mashiach. At the morning meal ... he says: This is the meal of the Holy Ancient One; Zeir Anpin and the field of holy apples come to dine with Him. It corresponds to Avraham, the pious elder, and through his merit one is saved from the judgment of Gehinnom.” The cited Lurianic text explicitly associates the morning meal with Abraham and the Holy Ancient One.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 60b, Beshalach 26:1–2 — “‘They went three days in the wilderness and found no water.’ Water means Torah. Who gave them Torah here? For the Torah had not yet been given to them. Rabbi Elazar said: They went out into the wilderness to contemplate, and the Holy One took the radiance of His glory from there; they went to contemplate Him but did not find Him. We have learned that the Holy One is called Torah, and water means Torah; Torah means the Holy One.” The original question explicitly addresses the fact that this episode precedes Sinai. Rav Tzadok follows its reading of the search for water as a search for the hidden radiance.

p: However, according to the parable of the Pesikta,
יֵשׁ לְהָבִין מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר אַחַר כָּךְ
we must understand what is said afterwards,
"You shall erase the memory of Amalek,"
that caused the coming of Amalek.
what use the remembrance will be,
how much is the grasp fitting for him
and what is above his portion
that he is permitted to contemplate.
On this it gives the advice,
"You shall erase the memory of Amalek":
at what one is not permitted
בָּא גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי קְלִיפַּת
as they said in the holy Zohar,
and when you erase the memory of Amalek,
beyond what you have been permitted,
for then you will attain fear of Heaven,
in the way that it is said,
and you will have uprightness of heart,
and you will have no yearning
for what you have not been permitted.
And this is what they said
"You shall erase the memory of Amalek," etc.,
you are the children of Avraham,
(and similarly in the Pesikta, ibid., siman 2).
שֶׁעִנְיַן שֶׁזָּכָה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
For the reason that Avraham Avinu, alav hashalom, merited
that he likened himself to ash.
And it is written (Mishlei 22:4), "The result of humility
וּכְתִיב [תְּהִלִּים יט, ט] פִּקּוּדֵי ה׳ יְשָׁרִים
and it is written (Tehillim 19:9), "The precepts of Hashem are upright,
only in one who makes himself
as if he does not exist
So too words of Torah are likened to water,
and go to a low place;
and they are likened to water, wine and milk,
only in the humblest of vessels;
so too words of Torah endure
only in one whose mind is lowly
which are upright and gladden the heart,
"And for the upright of heart, joy."
And by erasing the memory of Amalek
you will merit this, to be humble,
and you will merit to be upright and God-fearing,
and you will not wish to contemplate
anything but what you have been permitted,
that it is greater than what is said
for he said, "And what are we,"
as one who literally does not exist,
more than the image of "dust and ash,"
"And wisdom, from Ayin is it found";
"In all My house he is trusted;
פֶּה אֶל פֶּה אֲדַבֶּר בּוֹ וְגוֹמֵר
mouth to mouth do I speak with him," etc.
And at the morning meal of Shabbos,
when she is crowned with the Avos,

paragraphs.text: Sotah 21b:3 — “Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Hanina said: Words of Torah endure only in one who makes himself bare for them, as it is said, ‘I, wisdom, dwell with nakedness.’ Rabbi Yohanan said: Words of Torah endure only in one who makes himself as though he were nothing, as it is said, ‘Wisdom—from nothing is it found.’” The passage joins surrender for Torah with the humility expressed through the word “nothing.” Rav Tzadok connects this to Moses’ “What are we?”

paragraphs.text: Taanit 7a:15–16 — “Rabbi Hanina bar Idi said: Why are words of Torah compared to water? ... Just as water leaves a high place and goes to a low place, so words of Torah endure only in one whose mind is humble. Rabbi Oshaya said: Why are words of Torah compared to these three liquids—water, wine, and milk? ... Just as these three liquids are preserved only in the lowliest vessels, so words of Torah endure only in one whose mind is humble.” The images describe humility as the vessel that can retain Torah, rather than as an absence of understanding.

p: And it can further be said
that the remembrance of Amalek means
that a person should not be lenient with himself
even in a matter that seems light in his eyes.
in the realm of recognition and knowledge,
there branched out the coming of Amalek,
which brought about the dominion of the "first" of the kelipah,
and from this branched out the dominion
that branch out from his side;
and were it not for him,
as we said from the Gemara
and explained above at the end of Maamar 1),
כִּי כֹּחוֹ כּוֹלֵל כָּל שִׁבְעִים הַקְּלִיפּוֹת
for his power includes all seventy kelipos.
And from this a person will judge with his intellect
not to be lenient, chas v'shalom, in anything;
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא הִזְכִּיר כָּאן הַחֵטְא
and therefore it did not mention the sin here
For on the contrary, the essence of the remembrance is
שֶׁהָעוֹנֶשׁ בָּא עַל יְדֵי חֵטְא דַּק
that the punishment came through a subtle sin,
and from it branched out the coming of Amalek;
וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן יִהְיֶה בּוֹרֵחַ מִן הָעֲבֵירָה
and through this one will flee from transgression
and erases the memory of Amalek from the heart,

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Avodah Zarah 18a — “‘The iniquity of my heels surrounds me’: the sins a person tramples with his heels in this world surround him on the day of judgment.” The Gemara states the principle Rav Tzadok draws from Amalek. The sins a person treats as trivial bring the reckoning, so he may not be lenient in anything.
